Do not let any unreasonable feelings and thoughts sprout in the mind even for a moment. Constantly keep the mind empty, bright, and penetrating. Like a mirror set on its stand, it reflects whatever condition appears before it; it only reflects the condition before it and is not turned about by it. Beautiful or ugly is its own affair — what has it to do with me? It does not anticipate what comes, nor cling to what goes.”

If you wish to make true knowledge manifest, then in your daily use, whenever a thought stirs or words and deeds are produced, you should constantly raise awareness and illumination. Do not let any feeling or thought contrary to principle sprout in the mind even briefly. Constantly keep the mind empty, bright, and penetrating, like a bright mirror set on its stand: whatever is before it, it simply reflects it, without being dragged about by it. Whether it is beautiful or ugly is its own affair — what has it to do with me? When it comes, there is no expectation or waiting; when it goes, there is no affliction or clinging.
These few sentences are the key to cultivating the mind: let the true mind be master.

[Speech and action] Words and deeds. [Awareness and illumination] To know clearly what one’s present thought and emotion are. This is the basic skill of turning evil into good, delusion into awakening, and the ordinary into the sage. Hence the patriarchs and great masters often said: at all times and in all places, whatever karma one creates through body, mouth, and mind, one should all the while look back and know this mind. [Yan] Beautiful. [Chi
chī
] Ugly. [Anticipate] That is, “expect beforehand.”

“If unreasonable feelings and thoughts should stir even slightly, you should at once attack and govern them strictly, and wipe them out completely. It is like facing an enemy army: not only must you not let them invade your borders, you must also behead their generals and seize their banners, and wipe out the remaining bandits.”

If unreasonable feelings and thoughts have just begun to appear, you should at once attack and govern them strictly, and wipe them out completely. It is like facing an enemy army: not only must you not let them invade your territory, you must also behead their generals and seize their banners, wipe out the remaining bandits, and root them out entirely.
[Sprouting] Just beginning to appear. [Borders] A region handed over to an official to administer with full authority. [Qian
qiān
] To seize.
[In the method of commanding an army, one must be strict in governing oneself, neither slack nor careless. Subdue the self and return to propriety; hold fast to reverence and preserve sincerity.]

The method of commanding an army requires strict self-governance. One must be neither slack nor negligent, restraining one’s seeing, hearing, speaking, and acting so that they accord with the demands of “propriety,” reverent and utterly sincere.

[Wu (wú)] Do not. [Subduing the self and returning to propriety] A Confucian method of self-cultivation: restraining one’s seeing, hearing, speaking, and acting so that they accord with the demands of “propriety.” [Holding fast to reverence and preserving sincerity] Outwardly reverent, inwardly sincere.
[For one’s weapons one must use Yanzi’s four nevers, Zengzi’s three reflections, and Qu Boyu’s lessening of faults and knowing of wrongs.]
One’s weapons must be Yanzi’s four nevers, Zengzi’s three reflections, and Qu Boyu’s lessening of faults and knowing of wrongs.

[Weapons] Weapons. [Yanzi’s four nevers] Yanzi is Yan Hui, a disciple of Confucius. He was skilled in the work of mastering himself, strictly keeping to the four nevers: never look at what is contrary to propriety, never listen to it, never speak of it, never move in accord with it. [Zengzi’s three reflections] Zengzi, that is, Zeng Shen, a disciple of Confucius. He was skilled in the work of self-examination, saying, “I examine myself three times daily”: whether in planning for others I have been disloyal; whether in dealings with friends I have been untrustworthy; whether I have practiced what was transmitted to me — with these three he closely examined himself in body and mind. [Qu (
qú

) Boyu] A great officer of the state of Wei in the Spring and Autumn period, who daily reflected, examined, and corrected his faults — day after day, year after year, never a day without finding that he still had faults, never a day without bitterly repenting and amending. [Lessening of faults] To reduce one’s own faults. [Knowing of wrongs] To know one’s own faults.

[Add to this a trembling vigilance, as though standing on the brink of a deep abyss, as though treading on thin ice, and confront them so. Then the army’s might spreads afar and the band of thieves is chilled to the heart. They fear to incur the extreme punishment of the extinction of their kind, and hope to receive the great grace of pacification. From that time on they surrender one after another and submit to the highest transformation. They wholly reform their former minds and cultivate the virtue that follows.]

Add to this a trembling vigilance — as though standing on the brink of a deep abyss, as though treading on thin ice — and confront the army of thieves (deluded thoughts contrary to principle) with the utmost caution and solemn order. Then the army’s might spreads afar and the band of thieves is chilled to the heart. They dread suffering the calamity of the extinction of their kind and race, and hope for the great grace of pardon and pacification. And so they surrender one after another and submit, turn their minds about, wash their hearts and renew their faces, and become new people.

[Trembling with vigilance] Describes a manner of careful caution. [The band of thieves] Here “the band of thieves” means deluded thoughts contrary to principle. [Li (lí)] To suffer. [Cultivating his virtue] To restore one’s moral virtue. “Yu (
yù
)” is a classical particle; “Jue (
jué
)” means “his” or “its.”

[The general does not leave his door; the troops do not blood their blades. All foes become newborn babes; even rebels all become good subjects. Those above lead and those below follow; the whole land is clear and tranquil. Without moving shield or spear, one brings about great peace while seated.]

And so the general does not leave the camp gate, the troops do not shed blood in battle, and all foes and rebels become good and honest common people. High and low among the band of thieves follow one another’s example, all abandon evil and return to the right; the four seas are clear and tranquil, and without going to war the whole world is at peace.

[Newborn babe] A newly born infant; it is commonly used as a simile for one who is pure and good. [The whole land] Means “within the four seas.” The character “shuai” is pronounced “shuài” and means “all,” “every.”

This passage says that the key to attacking and subduing deluded thoughts contrary to principle is this: stand in strict formation and wait; the moment they begin to stir (this is the best moment to annihilate the enemy), strike them head-on at once and uproot them. People create evil through the actions of body, speech, and mind, and body and speech take mind as their root; hence to cut off evil by mindful awareness is like felling a poisonous tree by cutting straight through its root.

Because one’s skill in Buddha-recitation has now gained strength, deluded thoughts are few, and even when they arise they can be detected in good time. Every thought that arises must be examined in fine detail: is it greed, is it anger, or is it delusion, and why has it arisen? Dig out each root, one by one, and uproot it.
In the course of purifying the mind and gathering the provisions, the cultivation of patience is also most important.

Patience is the sharp weapon that shatters self-attachment, the foremost wondrous practice for attaining Buddhahood. Master Yongjia says in his Song of Enlightenment: “My teacher saw the Buddha Dipankara; for many kalpas he was the Ascetic of Patience.”

“Patience” means abiding peacefully in principle without the mind stirring. In fact, the whole of Buddhist study and practice is the cultivation of patience — not grasping at marks, thusness unmoved. As it is said, “The single word patience is the gate of all wonders.”

The cultivation of patience has four levels: the patience of submission, the patience of gentle compliance, the patience of non-arising, and the patience of quiescent extinction. The patience of submission is for the beginner, who must tame his mind and endure both favorable and adverse conditions. The patience of gentle compliance is when the mind has long been tamed, so that meeting with circumstances and conditions one can endure naturally without forced suppression; at this point the mind is gentle, harmonious, and well-disposed. The patience of non-arising is for those on the holy levels, who understand that all dharmas are from the outset unborn, that sentient and insentient alike are produced by conditions and without own-nature, empty just as they are; therefore within dharmas that lack own-nature the patient mind does not stir, and one personally realizes non-arising. The patience of quiescent extinction belongs to the sage at the fruit-stage, who thoroughly realizes the quiescent and extinguished realm of nirvāṇa, so that the two marks of motion and stillness both accord with thusness.

[No own-nature] Nature means essence; all dharmas have no substantial entity, and this is called having no own-nature. The Lotus Sutra says: “Know that all dharmas are always without own-nature.” The Śūraṅgama Sutra says: “All illusions are accomplished as without own-nature.”
As to why one should cultivate patience and how to cultivate it, Master Hanshan, in the Dream Journey Collection
Instructions to the Chan Adept Fajin, gives a penetrating teaching:

[All sentient beings’ equipment of birth, death, and suffering is accomplished through having a self; the unsurpassed bodhi, adorned with merit and wisdom, is arrived at through having no self. Because the self is set in opposition to things, right and wrong arise; right and wrong arising, love and hate are established; love and hate established, joy and anger proliferate; one’s own nature grows turbid and the ground of the mind grows dim; the ground of the mind dim, all evils grow; all evils growing, all sufferings gather; all sufferings gathering, birth and death are prolonged! All this is brought about by the self. How great is the harm done by the self! It is like a heavily fortified city with strong soldiers — how could it be broken easily!]

The reason all sentient beings have birth, death, and suffering is that these are established through having a self; the unsurpassed bodhi, adorned with merit and wisdom, is realized through having no self. When the self is made the center, one stands in opposition to others, and so right and wrong arise; right and wrong arising, love and hate are established; love and hate established, joy and anger proliferate. Then one’s own nature grows turbid and the ground of the mind grows dim; the ground of the mind dim, all evils grow; all evils growing, all sufferings gather; all sufferings gathering, the round of birth and death has no end! All of this is caused by having a “self.” How grave is the harm done by the self! Yet to break self-attachment is like attacking a fortress garrisoned by elite troops and closely defended — how could it be broken easily!
[Setting the self in opposition to things] To make the self the center and stand opposed to others. Here “things” means people other than oneself.

[Laozi has said: “The soft overcomes the hard; the weak overcomes the strong.” This is but the first stage of the practice of patience. Sentient beings rely on their self-view, which is firm and hard to break; therefore a single word of opposition they cannot accept, a single matter that goes against them they cannot bear, a single hunger or cold they cannot endure, a single thought of desire they cannot purify — all these are cases of not knowing the method of patience, merely increasing the attachment of self-view! Therefore the Buddha taught his disciples to cultivate the practice of harmony. He also said: “The patience of the dharma of suffering, the wisdom of the dharma of suffering.” And he also said: “The patience of the non-arising of dharmas is attained at the eighth ground.” From this we know that enduring from the patience of the arising of dharmas up to non-arising, the wondrous practice is perfected and the Buddha-fruit accomplished! The single practice of patience — how could it be shallow! Therefore it is said: in whatever one does, one should endure it.]

Laozi’s Daodejing says: “The soft overcomes the hard; the weak overcomes the strong.” This is the preliminary stage of the single practice of patience. The self-view that sentient beings hold is firm and hard to break. Therefore a single word of opposition they cannot accept, a single matter that goes against them they cannot bear, a single hunger or cold they cannot endure, a single thought of desire they cannot purify — all this is not knowing the method of patient endurance, but only continually strengthening the attachment to self-view! Therefore the Buddha taught his disciples to cultivate the practice of harmony. He also said: “The patience of the dharma of suffering, the wisdom of the dharma of suffering.” And again: “The patience of the non-arising of dharmas is realized only by a bodhisattva of the eighth ground.” From this we know that enduring from the patience of the arising of dharmas all the way to the patience of non-arising, the wondrous practice is perfected and the Buddha-fruit accomplished! The single practice of patience — how could it be a trifling matter! Therefore it is said: in whatever one does, one must be able to practice patience.

[Self-view] Also called self-attachment: the deluded clinging that takes the five aggregates of body and mind as a self. The Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment says: “All sentient beings, from beginningless time, have all manner of inversions, like a confused man who mistakes the four directions for one another (for example, taking east for west and south for north), and deludedly takes the four great elements as the mark of their own body and the shadowy traces of the six dusts as the mark of their own mind. It is like a diseased eye that sees flowers in the sky and a second moon. Good sons! The sky in truth has no flowers; it is the diseased one who deludedly clings. Because of deluded clinging, they are not only confused about the self-nature of this emptiness but also deluded about the place where the real flowers arise. From this deluded existence they revolve through birth and death, and this is called ignorance.” [The four great elements] Earth, water, fire, and wind. Earth takes hardness as its nature, water takes moisture, fire takes warmth, wind takes movement. All material forms in the world possess these four natures of hardness, moisture, warmth, and movement, and so they are called “great.” [Shadowy traces of the six dusts] The various thoughts produced when the six faculties come into contact with the six dusts; since these thoughts are all illusory and unreal, they are called the shadowy traces of the six dusts — the illusions conditioned by the six dusts. [Harmony] Harmony includes harmony in principle and harmony in affairs. Harmony in principle is the realization of cessation by choice: that is, everyone together practices and realizes this commonly chosen principle of quiescence. Harmony in affairs has six items, the so-called six points of reverent harmony: 1. harmony of body, dwelling together — the peaceful coexistence of bodies; 2. harmony of speech, no disputing — speech free of contention; 3. harmony of mind, shared joy — the mind’s common delight; 4. harmony of precepts, practicing together — common observance of the precepts; 5. harmony of views, common understanding — complete agreement in views; 6. harmony of benefit, equal sharing — benefit shared as one. [The patience of the dharma of suffering] In regard to the sufferings of the desire realm, the mind of wisdom abides peacefully in the principle of suchness. [The wisdom of the dharma of suffering] The uncontaminated wisdom obtained by contemplating the truth of suffering in the desire realm. [The patience of the arising of dharmas] All the kinds of patience prior to the patience of the non-arising of dharmas are called the patience of the arising of dharmas.

[Thus, wherever a thought stirs, test it with patience; wherever a foot is lifted, let patience go first; in every movement and expression, hold to patience; in joy, anger, sorrow, and delight, examine with patience. In this way the mind dares not stir wildly, the body dares not act wildly, affairs dare not be done wildly, feelings dare not be vented wildly. Therefore Laozi said: “Dare not be first in the world.” “Dare not” is another name for patience. Because one dares not be first in the world, patience is the foremost practice for attaining Buddhahood.]

Therefore, wherever a thought stirs, examine it with patience; wherever a foot is lifted, let patience walk ahead; in dealings with people and things, meet them with patience; in joy, anger, sorrow, and delight, test them with patience. In this way the mind dares not stir wildly, the body dares not act wildly, affairs dare not be done wildly, feelings dare not be vented wildly. Therefore Laozi’s Daodejing says: “Dare not be first in the world.” “Dare not” is another name for patience. Because one dares not, one therefore becomes first in the world. Thus patience is the foremost practice for attaining Buddhahood.

[Movement and expression] Bearing and conduct. [Dare not be first in the world] To wander through the world with an empty heart, without a self and so not opposed to things; things of themselves cannot overcome one. This is to be the highest among people.

[In this way patience is great and the self is small; therefore patience can clothe and cover me, and can also clothe and cover other things. For the virtue of benefiting self and others, nothing surpasses this. Hence it is said, “the garment of gentleness and patience” — this is the reason. The Chan monk asked for a Dharma phrase, and so I have entitled it: Patience as Your Garment. Chan monk, strive to put it into practice; do not take it as mere talk, and do not use it to win your bowl of rice.]

In this way patience is great and the self is small; therefore patience can shelter me and can also shelter others. For the virtue of benefiting self and others, nothing surpasses patience. Hence the saying that one should take gentleness and patience as one’s garment — this is the very reason! The Chan monk Fajin asked for a Dharma phrase, and so I have entitled it: Patience as Your Garment. Fajin, you must strive to put it into practice! Never think it a commonplace, and never use it as a tool for winning fame and profit.

[The garment of patience] The mind of patience, because it can guard against all outer obstructions, is likened to a garment. [Mere talk] A set phrase forever on the lips. [Bo] To exchange for. [Not to use it to win your bowl of rice] Here Master Hanshan warns with deep earnestness: to study and understand the principle, one must practice it oneself; never fail to do it oneself while using it to teach others, making it a tool for winning fame and profit. In the Analects,

Xian Wen, it says: “The learning of the ancients was for themselves; the learning of people today is for others.” The Analects with Commentary and Subcommentary says: “The learning of the ancients was to tread and practice it, and this was for themselves. The learning of people today is merely to speak of it to others while unable to practice it themselves, and this is for others. Fan Ye says: ‘To be for others is to rely on reputation to display oneself to things; to be for oneself is to accord with the Way through the mind.’” [To rely on reputation to display oneself to things] To use reputation to display oneself to others — that is, to fish for fame and reputation. “Feng” is anciently the same as “ping,” to rely on, to depend on. “Things” means people other than oneself.

In the course of purifying the mind and gathering the provisions, one follows conditions to dissolve karma by holding the Buddha’s name; this is to cultivate one mind undisturbed amid actual combat. Moreover, doing so makes one’s life smoother and more peaceful and happy, paves the way for right mindfulness at the moment of death, and prevents karmic obstacles from manifesting at that time.

When a deluded thought arises, that is precisely a condition for turning and dissolving karma; one must seize the opportunity at once to turn and dissolve it. Each time karma is turned, the karmic seed is weakened somewhat. Turning continually, it is continually weakened, until it is uprooted.

The patriarchs say: “Follow conditions to dissolve old karma, and create no new calamity.” Therefore whenever a karmic seed comes into activity, one should take this opportunity to weaken it, even to uproot it. Conversely, if one follows one’s habitual tendencies, one creates new calamity, and the karmic seed grows stronger still, so that when it later erupts it is harder to control.

When a deluded thought arises, this is karma binding the mind; to replace the deluded thought with the Buddha’s name is the mind turning karma. At all times and in all places, replace deluded thoughts with the Buddha’s name: if ten recitations will not do, take up ten more; continue in this way, ceaselessly turning karma with the mind. As days pass and the practice deepens, the wonder of it cannot be spoken. The Caigentan says: “At the place where a thought arises, as soon as you notice it heading down the road of desire, pull it back onto the road of principle. As soon as it arises, be aware; as soon as you are aware, turn it about. This is the juncture at which calamity is turned into blessing, at which the dead come back to life — never let it slip by lightly!”

Remember: follow the stream of presently active thoughts and purify away deluded thinking and the habitual tendencies of greed, anger, and delusion. Let no thought be let pass; let every thought be seen through.
When the practice is deep, karma dissolves and wisdom shines clear, obstacles are exhausted and blessings mount high; the joy of it cannot be described.
For the way of dissolving karma and eliminating habitual tendencies, see in detail
Mind, Self-Nature, and Tathāgatagarbha
, the section “How the Consciousness-Mind Operates,” and
The Mind Can Transform Karma
Question: I have resolved to make rebirth in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss my foremost concern. Please tell me the method of practice that gives the surest rebirth.
Answer: One must constantly examine oneself: am I cultivating pure karma or creating the karma of the round of rebirth; is the mind turning karma, or is karma binding the mind? (See in detail
The Mind Can Transform Karma
.) As for the specific method of practice, Master Hanshan teaches:
“As for the final, ultimate great matter
(the great matter of rebirth at the end of life)
, the work to be done is all the more intimate. Each day, apart from the two periods
(morning and evening)

of the daily liturgy, throughout the six periods of day and night simply place the single sound of Amitābha Buddha across your chest, never forgetting it from thought to thought, never dimming it from mind to mind.
Give no thought to any worldly affair, but take the single phrase of the Buddha’s name as your own root of life.
(The root of life means that without it one cannot live.)

Grit your teeth and resolve never to let it go, so that whether eating, drinking, rising, or resting, walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, this single sound of the Buddha is ever present before you. If you meet with adverse or favorable conditions, with joy or anger, with afflictions, and your mind is unpeaceable, then take this
(this)
single sound of the Buddha and raise it with a jab — and you will see the affliction vanish on the spot. Because thought-after-thought affliction is the root of the suffering of birth and death
(because thought
after thought
of affliction is the root of the suffering of birth and death)
; now, by reciting the Buddha’s name to destroy affliction
(that is, now using thought-after-thought Buddha-recitation to destroy affliction)

, this is where the Buddha saves us from the suffering of birth and death. If by Buddha-recitation one can dissolve affliction, then one can be free of birth and death; there is no other method. If by Buddha-recitation one can be master of affliction, then one can be master in dreams; if one can be master in dreams, then one can be master amid the suffering of illness; if one can be master amid the suffering of illness, then at the approach of death one will be clear and lucid and will know where one is going. This matter is not hard to do; it is only that one thought must be urgent regarding birth and death, and that one must simply lean firmly on the single sound of the Buddha, never seeking elsewhere in thought. When it has long been pure and familiar, one will naturally attain great peace, ease, and freedom, and gain great joy and benefit — truly not to be compared with the pleasures of the five desires of the world. May Your Highness give heed to this method; this is true practice, and apart from it there is nothing more direct and economical than this. Never listen to wrong views and false teachings and be misled by them.”
(Dream Roaming Collection: Reply to the Question of Prince De)
Master Hanshan also says:

“When the practice gains strength, outer conditions no longer enter; only the afflictions within the mind arise without form or cause. Sometimes thoughts of desire break out, sometimes the mind grows fretful and depressed, sometimes all kinds of obstacles arise, until the mind is weary and the strength exhausted, and there is nothing to be done. These are the eighth consciousness
(the ālaya-consciousness)

in which are stored the seeds of habitual tendencies from immeasurable kalpas; today, pressed hard by the practice, they all emerge. At this point one must be most clear-headed: first one must see through them and pass beyond them; never allow oneself to be shrouded by them, never allow oneself to be toyed with by them, never take them as real things. Simply rouse your spirit, rouse your courage, and raise the huatou of your own inquiry
(the reciter of the Buddha’s name raises the Buddha’s name)
. Right at the place where such thoughts arise, press on and pursue them without letup: here in me there was originally no such thing
here originally there is no such thing
, and ask it
(it)

whence it comes. What after all is it? You must resolve to see where it comes to rest. Pressing on in this way, you will make gods and ghosts alike weep and hide their traces. Drive them all out and slay them utterly, leaving not a thread behind. Striving in this way, you will naturally see the good news.”
(Dream Roaming Collection: Reply to Vice Censor-in-Chief Zheng Kunyan)
If one can practice according to
Master Shandao’s teaching

thought after thought without interruption, making the end of life the limit; ... in walking, standing, sitting, and lying down, one must sharpen the mind and subdue oneself, ceasing neither day nor night
, then the effect of purifying the mind and gathering the provisions is the best, and the method is the most single-minded. Master Shandao says:
Precisely because calling the name is easy
(precisely because calling the name is easier than visualization)
continuous recitation brings rebirth
If one can continue thought after thought, making the end of life the limit
, then ten out of ten are reborn, a hundred out of a hundred are reborn.
May all people reflect well within themselves:
in walking, standing, sitting, and lying down, one must sharpen the mind and subdue oneself, ceasing neither day nor night
(See in detail
Master Shandao’s Pure Land Teaching

blocks.text: Chapter Nine: Rejoicing in the Pure Land and Wearying of Saṃsāra

inline.s: The sufferings of the Saha world are too bitter for words; the joys of the Pure Land are too joyful to describe.

rows.s: the more so when pressed by illness;
1. The Root of Birth and Death
2. Severing Love and Focusing the Thought
4. Taking No Concern in a Hundred Matters

inline.s: Faith, vows, and practice are the three provisions of the Pure Land school. Among them, vows mean rejoicing in the Pure Land and wearying of Saṃsāra. Therefore, while reciting the Buddha’s name with diligence, the reciter must also cultivate the practice of rejoicing and wearying, and put it into effect in daily life; this is the concrete expression of faith and vows.

Why should one rejoice in the Pure Land? Because “the sentient beings in that land have no suffering at all, but receive every joy” — and still more because this is the golden highway that fulfills the bodhi-vow to “save all sentient beings and together accomplish the Buddha Way”!
In the Buddha Speaks the Amitābha Sutra, the Buddha says:
Śāriputra, why is that land called Ultimate Bliss? Because the sentient beings in that land have no suffering at all, but receive every joy; therefore it is called Ultimate Bliss.

As for “all suffering,” there are the three sufferings, the eight sufferings, the ten sufferings, and the hundred and ten sufferings; and there is also the suffering of the two kinds of birth and death (fragmentary birth-and-death and transformational birth-and-death).

The three sufferings are the suffering of suffering, the suffering of decay, and the suffering of process. First, the suffering of suffering: beings in the world have bodies subject to birth and death, which is suffering enough; when the various sufferings press and scorch them besides, it is suffering added to suffering, and so it is called the suffering of suffering. Second, the suffering of decay: the suffering felt when a state of happiness that has come about by chance is once lost. Third, the suffering of process: the suffering of all formations being impermanent, flowing on without cease, and never able to be still.

The eight sufferings are: 1. the suffering of birth — the pain at the time of birth; 2. the suffering of aging — the pain of old age and bodily weakness; 3. the suffering of illness — the pain of sickness; 4. the suffering of death — the pain at the approach of death; 5. the suffering of separation from the loved — the pain of parting from those one loves; 6. the suffering of meeting the hateful — the pain of being together with enemies; 7. the suffering of not getting what one seeks — the pain of desires unfulfilled; 8. the suffering of the blazing five aggregates — because of the illusory and false dharmas of body and mind belonging to the five aggregates (form, feeling, perception, formation, consciousness), one gives rise to delusion and creates karma amid the objects of the six dusts, and is thoroughly scorched, like a blazing fire that cannot be stopped.

[The five yin] The old translation of the five aggregates. Yin means concealment: it can conceal and cover the dharma-nature of suchness and give rise to afflictions. [The five aggregates] The aggregate of form, the aggregate of feeling, the aggregate of perception, the aggregate of formation, the aggregate of consciousness. These five are produced by accumulation, and so are called the “five aggregates”; they can also cover over people’s true nature, causing them to be deluded and inverted and to create all kinds of karma, and so they are also called the “five yin.” Among them, the aggregate of form refers to matter and is called “form-dharma”; the four aggregates of feeling, perception, formation, and consciousness belong to the mental and are called “mind-dharma.” These are the five great elements that make up body and mind. Among them, the aggregate of form is the body, and the remaining four aggregates (feeling, perception, formation, consciousness) are the mind.
Concerning the ten sufferings and the hundred and ten sufferings, Master Lianchi says in his Commentary and Subcommentary on the Buddha Speaks the Amitābha Sutra:

“The ten sufferings: the Sutra of the Bodhisattva Treasury says, 1. the suffering of birth, 2. the suffering of aging, and so on up to 10. the suffering of revolving in birth and death. The hundred and ten sufferings: the Yogācārabhūmi says, 1. the suffering of undifferentiated revolution, 2. the suffering of desire, 3. the suffering of delusion, and so on up to fifty-five sufferings; then nine kinds of suffering, and within those nine, further opened out in turn into fifty-five, which together make a hundred and ten sufferings.”

None of the sufferings above exists at all in the Land of Ultimate Bliss. As for the suffering of the two kinds of birth and death: one who is reborn in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss is born transformationally from a lotus, and so has no fragmentary birth-and-death; moreover, one ascends to the stage of non-retrogression — why worry about the suffering of transformational birth-and-death? Hence it is said, “there is no suffering at all.”

[The two kinds of birth and death] Fragmentary birth-and-death and transformational birth-and-death. [Fragmentary birth-and-death] For sentient beings in the three realms and six paths, because of the karma of good and evil they have drawn, their lifespans all have limits and their bodily forms all have divisions; therefore their birth and death is called “fragmentary birth-and-death.” One who ends fragmentary birth-and-death escapes the round of rebirth and leaves the three realms. [Transformational birth-and-death] For the sages of the three vehicles, who have already cut off the delusions of view and thought and ended fragmentary birth-and-death, in the course of cultivating the Way deluded thinking gradually ceases and realization gradually increases; each period of this shifting between delusion and realization is different, and the passing from the earlier period into the later is just like one birth and death. Its transformations are wondrous and unfathomable, inconceivable, and so it is called “transformational birth-and-death.” One who ends transformational birth-and-death perfectly realizes the Buddha-fruit.
The Buddha Speaks the Amitābha Sutra
says:
“But receive every joy.”
As for “every joy,” the Repentance Master Ciyun, comparing the sufferings of this land with the joys of that land, speaks of ten kinds:

First, this land has the suffering of not always meeting a Buddha; that land has none, but has the joy of seeing the Buddha when the lotus opens and always being able to draw near to him. Second, this land has the suffering of not hearing the Dharma taught; that land has none, but has the joy of water, birds, and trees all proclaiming the wondrous Dharma. Third, there is no suffering of being entangled by evil friends, but there is the joy of all the superior good people assembling in one place. Fourth, there is no suffering of being harassed and disordered by hordes of demons, but there is the joy of being protected in mind by all Buddhas and kept far from demonic affairs. Fifth, there is no suffering of unceasing revolution in birth and death, but there is the joy of cutting across birth and death and forever escaping the round of rebirth. Sixth, there is no suffering of being unable to avoid the three evil paths, but there is the joy that the evil paths are forever left behind and even their names are not heard. Seventh, there is no suffering of the dusts of conditions obstructing the Way, but there is the joy of enjoying things naturally without needing to manage them. Eighth, there is no suffering of a short lifespan, but there is the joy of a lifespan equal to the Buddha’s, with no limit at all. Ninth, there is no suffering of falling back in practice, but there is the joy of entering the company of the definitely settled and never turning back. Tenth, there is no suffering that dusty kalpas make accomplishment difficult, but there is the joy that in one lifetime one’s practice is complete and what is to be done is done.

[The definitely settled group] One of the three groups. [The three groups] The three groups are three kinds of sentient beings: the definitely settled group, the wrongly settled group, and the unsettled group. The definitely settled group refers to those sentient beings who will certainly realize enlightenment; the wrongly settled group refers to those who ultimately cannot realize enlightenment; the unsettled group refers to those between the two, who may or may not realize enlightenment.
[Dusty kalpas] That is,

the three-thousand dust-mote kalpa: all the things of one three-thousand-great-thousand world are ground into ink, and a dot is made for each three-thousand-great-thousand world passed; when the ink is used up, all the worlds passed are again shattered into motes of dust, and each mote of dust is then counted as one kalpa — this is a simile expressing an extremely long span of time.
The Precious Mirror of the Lotus School says:

“In the turbid realm of the Saha world, sufferings gather and the pursuit of the Way is hard to accomplish; in the joyful land of the Pure Land, all good gathers and one ascends to the stage of non-retrogression. Those who call the name are protected in mind by all Buddhas and attain rebirth; those who give rise to bodhi are illumined by Amitābha’s light and advance. Bodhisattvas and arhats are one’s fellow travelers
(companions)

, and water, birds, and trees all recite the Buddha’s name. The ear constantly hears the wondrous Dharma, and the mind at once cuts off greed and anger. Joy is without end; how could the measure of life be exhausted? As soon as one is born in that land one at once attains A-wei
(A-wei-yue-zhi, also rendered A-pi-ba-zhi, meaning non-retrogression from Buddhahood; this is an important stage in the course of a bodhisattva’s practice)

— how can it be compared with the paths of gods and humans, where at every turn there is much opposition and compliance? On the road of the provisional vehicles, the roots of goodness are rarely complete; the three worthy ones before the grounds have not yet seen the Way and already lose mindfulness. ... From this we know that the followers of the three vehicles, passing through seng-qi kalpas
(a-seng-qi kalpas, that is, asaṃkhyeya kalpas)

, accomplish nothing in practice; whereas the gate of Buddha-recitation, in the snap of a finger, reaches the stage of non-retrogression. Therefore those born in the Pure Land, because they are only good and without evil, never fall back from their stage, and are certain to attain Buddhahood. Hence the Amitābha Sutra says: in the Land of Ultimate Bliss, all who are born there are A-pi-ba-zhi. Alas! The faith of beginners is shallow, and without other-power it is hard to advance in practice; our Buddha’s vow is deep, and all who have the condition are gathered in. You must believe that learning the Way through other gates is like an ant
(a tiny insect)

climbing a high mountain, while rebirth in the Pure Land is like a sailboat running with the current. Amitābha welcomes and guides one straight to bodhi; the sages support one, lifting one above the three realms. The highest grade at once attains the Buddha-fruit; even the lowest birth exceeds the heavenly palaces. Believe universally and doubt not; practice together without retreat.”

[Provisional vehicles] The bodhisattvas of the provisional vehicles are the bodhisattvas of the Tripitaka, Shared, and Distinct teachings; because their practice is still shallow, they have truly not yet reached the position of a real bodhisattva. [The three worthy ones] In the course of Mahāyāna cultivation, among the fifty-two positions from ordinary being to sage, the bodhisattvas of the ten abodes, ten practices, and ten dedications have only cut off the delusions of view and thought, and still have the delusion of dust-motes and the delusion of ignorance; they have not entered the holy position of the ten grounds, and so they are called only the “three worthy ones,” or “bodhisattvas before the grounds.”
Master Yinguang teaches:
“The sufferings of the Saha world are too bitter for words; the joys of the Pure Land are too joyful to describe.”

He also sets these two worlds in sharp contrast, pointing out that one should make a sincere and earnest vow, vowing to leave the sufferings of the Saha world and to attain the joys of the Pure Land. His words are:

“The sufferings of the Saha world are immeasurable and boundless. To sum them up, they do not go beyond the eight sufferings, namely birth, aging, illness, death, separation from the loved, meeting the hateful, not getting what one seeks, and the blazing of the five aggregates. These eight sufferings are possessed by all alike, from one at the height of honor for a time to the beggar at the lowest. The first seven are the fruits drawn by past lives; when pondered deeply they are known of themselves and need no detailed explanation — to explain would waste too much ink. The eighth, ‘the suffering of the blazing five aggregates,’ is the cause of future suffering in the arising of thoughts and the stirring of mind now, and in one’s movements and actions. Cause and effect are linked and continue without interruption, and from kalpa to kalpa none can be freed. The five aggregates are form, feeling, perception, formation, and consciousness. Form is the body that the karmic retribution has drawn; feeling, perception, formation, and consciousness are the illusory and false mind that arises on contact with objects. Through these illusory and false dharmas of body and mind, one gives rise to delusion and creates karma amid the objects of the six dusts, like a fire blazing up that cannot be stopped, and so it is called blazing. Furthermore, ‘yin’ means covering, and its sound and meaning are the same as “shade.” Through these five dharmas the true nature is covered over and cannot appear. It is like thick clouds hiding the sun: though the sun’s radiance is bright
(gǎo means bright)
, it suffers no loss at all, yet because the clouds cover it, its light is not received. Ordinary people who have not cut off delusion and karma are obstructed and covered by these five dharmas
(form, feeling, perception, formation, and consciousness)

, and the sky of their nature and the sun of their wisdom cannot appear — just the same. This eighth suffering is the root of all sufferings. One who cultivates the Way, with deep power of concentration, becomes utterly unattached amid the objects of the six dusts and does not give rise to hatred or love. Applying effort and practice further from this point, one advances to realize non-arising, and then delusion and karma are utterly purified and the root of birth and death is cut off. Yet this work is by no means easy; in the age of decline, those who attain it are truly rare. Therefore one must devote oneself single-mindedly to the pure karma and seek rebirth in the Pure Land, relying on the Buddha’s compassionate power to be reborn in the West. Once reborn, one is born transformationally from a lotus and has no suffering of birth. Of pure youthful appearance, with a lifespan equal to empty space, the body knows no calamity or change, no aging, illness, or death — their names are not even heard, much less their reality. One follows the assembly of sages and personally attends upon Amitābha; water, birds, and trees all proclaim the sounds of Dharma, and according to one’s own faculties one realizes through hearing. Even those one holds dear are utterly unobtainable, much less could there be enemies. Think of clothing and clothing comes; think of food and food comes; the towers, halls, and dwellings are all made of the seven treasures, not wrought by human effort but transformed at will. Thus the seven sufferings of the Saha world are turned about to become seven joys. As for the body, one has great supernormal powers and great might, and without leaving where one is, in a single thought one can perform all Buddha-works throughout the Buddha-worlds of the ten directions, seeking the Way above and transforming beings below. As for the mind, one has great wisdom and great eloquence, and within one dharma comprehends the true aspect of all dharmas, expounding the Dharma according to faculties without any error. Even when speaking in worldly terms, one accords with the wondrous principle of true aspect. One has no suffering of the blazing five aggregates, but enjoys the joy of the quiescence of body and mind. Hence the sutra says, ‘there is no suffering at all, but only the reception of every joy; therefore it is called Ultimate Bliss.’” “Now that you know the Saha world is suffering and the Pure Land is joy, you should make a sincere and earnest vow, vowing to leave the sufferings of the Saha world and to attain the joys of the Pure Land. The urgency of that vow should be like that of one who has fallen into a latrine pit yearning to get out, or of one imprisoned yearning for home.”
(from the Record of Master Yinguang’s Excellent Words)

blocks.text: The More So When Pressed by Illness

inline.s: Qing
(the Qing dynasty)
Master Daoche was a man of Qiantang. Leaving home, he studied under a master and uncovered the originally possessed
(seeing the nature)
. Afterward he devoted himself single-mindedly to the pure karma. He lived at Mañjuśrī Hermitage in Hangzhou, and setting a fixed term
(a prearranged term)
, entered closed retreat. In his room there was nothing superfluous
(there were no extra things in the retreat room)
, with but one table and one couch
(only a small table and a bed)
. After only a few days he fell ill and was in great distress
(only a few days into the retreat
he fell ill, and it grew more and more serious)
, he roused himself
(exhorted himself)
saying: “Reciting the Buddha’s name is precisely for birth and death
(reciting the Buddha’s name in retreat is precisely in order to end birth and death)
. How can I stop because of illness
chuò
: to cease)
(how could one stop the retreat and go seek medical treatment because of illness?)
” He held the Buddha’s name more earnestly than ever. Before long
(not long after)
golden light illumined the room, the Buddha stroked his crown, and the illness was cured at once.
Thus he attained the samādhi of Buddha-recitation; walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, he had not a single alien thought. So it was for three years; on the full-moon day of the third month
(the fifteenth day of the third lunar month)
he left the retreat. Having ascended the seat and finished expounding the Dharma, he said to the assembly: “I shall, on the full-moon day of the seventh month
(the fifteenth day of the seventh month)
, return to the West; you may all come to see me off.” When the time came
(when the fifteenth day of the seventh month arrived)
, just as
(just when)
the Ullambana assembly was being held and the assembly had gathered
(the people had gathered together)
, someone brought up his earlier words
(someone mentioned that the Master had said some days earlier that he would attain rebirth after the fifteenth of the seventh month)
, and the Master said: “There is such a matter
(there is indeed such a matter)

. Wait a little.” The next day he handed over the abbotship, held a vegetarian feast to take leave of the assembly, entered his niche, sat with eyes closed, and his breath ceased. After a while he revived
(after a moment he came to again)
and said: “Parting far from you all, could I be without a word?
The sufferings of the Saha world cannot be told; the joys of the Pure Land cannot be told

. If you would remember me, simply recite Amitābha Buddha, and before long we shall meet again. If you miss this life, you will revolve through the long night — how painful, how painful!” Having spoken, he passed away, aged forty-eight.
(from the Record of Pure Land Sages and Worthies)

[The Ullambana assembly] “Ullambana” is rendered into Chinese as “releasing the upside-down.” When people die and fall into the three evil paths, they suffer extremely, as if hung upside down. “Pen” is the vessel that holds food. “Ullambana” means: filling vessels with all kinds of precious and delicious foods to offer to the Buddhas and the Saṃgha, and relying on the inconceivable power of the field of merit of the Three Jewels to rescue the former dead from the suffering of being hung upside down. The “Ullambana assembly” is the Dharma assembly held every year on the fifteenth day of the seventh lunar month, at which all kinds of offerings are abundantly prepared and presented to the Three Jewels in order to rescue the former dead from the suffering of being hung upside down.
Master Yinguang says: “
When one who recites the Buddha’s name falls ill, one should single-mindedly await death. If one’s allotted lifespan is not yet exhausted, one will quickly recover, because
(because)
reciting the Buddha’s name with body and mind wholly let go is the most powerful way to dissolve karma, and when karma is dissolved the illness is cured. If one does not let go but wishes to get well
(wishes for the illness to be cured)
, then if one cannot get well, one will certainly have no way to attain rebirth, because one is unwilling to be reborn
(because one is unwilling to seek rebirth)

. If one does not understand these principles, how can one still rely on the Buddha’s compassionate power? As for your mother’s illness, you should earnestly urge her to let go and seek rebirth; if her lifespan is not exhausted, seeking rebirth will instead bring a swift cure, for because the mind is utterly sincere, she will receive the Buddha’s compassionate blessing.”
(from the Collected Writings of Master Yinguang: Letter in Reply to the Brothers Zhou Mengyou)
Master Shandao says:

“Whoever, at the end of life, wishes to be born in the Pure Land must not fear death. Constantly reflect that this body is full of suffering, entangled in all manner of impure evil karma; if one can cast off this foul body, transcend birth and be born in the Pure Land, receive immeasurable joy, and be freed from the bitter course of birth and death, that is a matter of satisfaction — like taking off worn-out clothes and getting to change into precious garments. Simply let go of body and mind, and do not give rise to attachment. Whenever illness comes, reflect on impermanence and single-mindedly await death.”
(from Master Shandao’s Text on Right Mindfulness for Rebirth at the End of Life)

[Impermanence] All dharmas in the world arise and cease, shift and flow, and do not abide for a single instant: this is called impermanence. Impermanence is the mark of this Saha world. For living things, plants and animals (human beings among them), there is birth, aging, illness, and death; for lifeless minerals, implements, and even mountains, rivers, and the great earth, there is formation, abiding, decay, and emptiness. To know impermanence thoroughly is to understand that whatever is born must perish, whatever gathers must scatter, whatever rises must fall; that all things will pass, and in the blink of an eye all is empty. Ending birth and death is then the foremost matter, and one will no longer give rise to greedy love for pleasant things and situations, nor to anger toward irritating things and situations — for greed and anger are the root of the round of birth and death. At the same time, to know impermanence thoroughly is to warn and spur oneself at every moment: life is short and the land is fragile; one must seize the time to practice, for when a single breath does not come, one belongs to the next life.
All things that pass before the eye are sorted as fair and foul; / when the end comes, not one of them concerns you at all.

Among the three provisions of the Pure Land — faith, vows, and practice — vows mean wearying of the Saha world and rejoicing in the Pure Land. Therefore the reciter of the Buddha’s name must not only rejoice in the Pure Land but also weary of the Saha world; this is most important. Master Xingce, the tenth patriarch of the Pure Land school, says:
“With a true and real vow, give rise to a mind of rejoicing
(xīn, the same as “xin,” to rejoice)

and renunciation, seeing the three realms as a prison, seeing home as shackles, seeing sounds and forms as poisoned wine, seeing fame and profit as ropes and locks, seeing the successes and failures of several decades as last night’s dream, seeing this one lifetime of karmic life in the Saha world as a stay at an inn — believing that one puts off this body here and leaves it, and single-mindedly reciting the Buddha’s name alone, vowing to be born together in the Pure Land.” “That Buddha-recitation may not leave one’s practice in vain: one must diligently spur body and mind, and cherish even an inch of time. How much more, when life hangs on a breath — how could it last long? Like a prisoner going to the market, step by step he nears death.
One must earnestly and ceaselessly
(diligent without cease)
day and night, toiling
kū kū
, laboring without slack)
through heat and cold,
with the single great name of the Buddha without a moment’s pause, and rebirth in the Pure Land is certain. Take care not to be keen at the start and slack at the end.”
(from the Essence of Master Xingce’s Admonitions)
Master Guangqin says:

“If emotional attachment is not cut off, then even while reciting the Buddha’s name with the mouth, thought after thought still falls into the Saha world. If one is earnest and utterly sincere and lets go of the ten thousand conditions, then in a single thought one can arrive in the West. But if the ten thousand conditions pull and tug and cannot be relinquished, then a hundred years or ten thousand years will still be within the three realms.”
Then how, amid the pull and tug of the ten thousand conditions, can one accomplish the wearying of the Saha world? Here I transcribe and annotate the relevant teachings of the patriarchs as follows.
Master Hanshan, in the Dream Roaming Collection
Essential Pointers on Buddha-Recitation, says:

[The single gate of reciting the Buddha’s name and seeking rebirth in the Pure Land was originally meant to settle the great matter of birth and death. Hence it is said: recite the Buddha’s name to end birth and death. When people of today give rise to the aspiration, it is because they wish to end birth and death that they are willing to recite the Buddha’s name, saying only that ‘the Buddha can end birth and death.’ But if one does not know the root-stock of birth and death, toward what after all does one recite? If the mind that recites the Buddha’s name cannot cut off the root-stock of birth and death, how can birth and death be ended?]

This Dharma gate of reciting the Buddha’s name and seeking rebirth in the Pure Land was originally meant to settle the great matter of birth and death. Hence it is said: recite the Buddha’s name to end birth and death. When people of today give rise to the aspiration, it is because they wish to end birth and death that they are willing to recite the Buddha’s name, saying only that ‘Buddha-recitation can end birth and death.’ But if one does not know the root of birth and death, toward what after all does one recite? If the mind that recites the Buddha’s name cannot cut off the root of birth and death, how then can birth and death be ended?
[Root-stock] The root and trunk of a plant; a simile for the foundation of a thing.

[What is the root-stock of birth and death? The ancients said: “If one’s karma were not heavy, one would not be born in the Saha world; if one’s love were not cut off, one would not be born in the Pure Land.” From this we know that the root of love is the root-stock of birth and death. For all sentient beings suffer the suffering of birth and death through the fault of love and desire. If we trace this root of love, it is not something that began in this life, nor in one, two, three, or four lives; it is that from beginningless time, since birth and death first were, life after life, casting off one body and receiving another, all has been the revolution of love and desire, right down to today. Reflecting back on the past, was there ever a single thought that briefly left this root of love? The seeds of this root of love have been accumulated deep through kalpas, and so birth and death are endless.]

What is the root of birth and death? The ancients said: “If one’s karma were not heavy, one would not be born in the Saha world; if one’s love were not cut off, one would not be born in the Pure Land.” From this we know that the root of love is the root of birth and death. For all sentient beings suffer the suffering of birth and death through the fault of love and desire. If we trace this root of love, it is not something that exists only in this life, nor in one, two, three, or four lives; it is that from beginningless time, since birth and death first were, life after life, casting off the body (death) and receiving a body (taking rebirth), all has been the revolution of love and desire, right down to today. Reflecting back on the past, was there ever a single thought that briefly left this root of love? The seeds of this root of love have been accumulated deep through numberless kalpas, and therefore birth and death are without end.
[Love] The meaning of greedy attachment and defilement.
The Compendium of the Meaning of the Mahāyāna says: “Greed and defilement are called love.” The Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment says: “The round of rebirth has love as its root.”
[The root of love] Love produces karmic fruit, and so it is called the root of love.
Master Xing’an says: “Reciting the Buddha’s name is no hard task; / the hard part is a single mind. / A single mind is no hard task; / the hard part is to sever love’s root.”

[People today have only just now given rise to the aspiration to recite the Buddha’s name, and they seek rebirth in the West into empty space; they do not even know the name of the fact that love is the root of birth and death — how could they ever have cut off a single thought? Since they do not know the root of birth and death, then while reciting the Buddha’s name on the one hand, they simply let the root of birth and death grow on the other. Reciting the Buddha’s name in this way has nothing to do with birth and death. In such a case, no matter how you recite, when you recite to the moment of death you will see only the root of love of birth and death appear before you; then you will know that the Buddha was of no help at all, and you will resent the Buddha-recitation for having no efficacy — but repentance will be too late.]

People today have only just now given rise to the aspiration to recite the Buddha’s name; they merely seek rebirth in the West into empty space, and do not even know that love is the root of birth and death. How could they ever have cut off a single thought? Since they do not know what the root of birth and death is, then while reciting the Buddha’s name on the one hand, they simply let the root of birth and death (love) grow on the other. Reciting the Buddha’s name in this way has nothing to do with ending birth and death. In such a case, no matter how you recite, when you recite to the moment of death you will see only the root of birth and death (love) appear before you; then you will know that the Buddha-recitation was of no help at all, and you will resent it for having no efficacy — but repentance will be too late.

[Therefore I urge those who recite the Buddha’s name today to first know that love is the root of birth and death. And now, in reciting the Buddha’s name, thought after thought one must cut off this root of love. Even in one’s daily life as a householder reciting the Buddha’s name, when the eye sees children and grandchildren, family ties and property, there is not one thing that is not love, and so there is no affair and no thought that is not the business of birth and death — one is like a whole body in a pit of fire. One does not know that even while reciting the Buddha’s name, the root of love in the mind has never once been let go. It is just that while reciting one says one’s recitation is not earnest, not knowing that love is the master and Buddha-recitation is the surface. Reciting in this way, the Buddha is merely recited while love is merely allowed to grow. Moreover, when the affection for children appears, turn the light around and look: can this single recitation of the Buddha really hold its own against this love? Can it really cut off this love? If it cannot cut off this love, how after all can birth and death be ended? Because the conditions of love have been familiar through many lives, while Buddha-recitation has only just been aspired to and is very unfamiliar, and is not earnest and solid besides, therefore it has no power.]

Therefore I urge those who recite the Buddha’s name today to first know that love is the root of birth and death. And now, in reciting the Buddha’s name, thought after thought one must cut off this root of love. Even in one’s daily life as a householder reciting the Buddha’s name, when the eye sees children and grandchildren, family ties and property, there is not one thing that is not love, and so there is no affair and no thought that is not the business of birth and death — one is like a whole body in a pit of fire. Yet one does not know that even while reciting the Buddha’s name, the root of love in the mind has never once been let go. It is just that while reciting one says one’s recitation is not earnest, not knowing the reason within: love is the master and Buddha-recitation is the surface. Reciting in this way, the Buddha is merely recited while love is merely allowed to grow. Moreover, when the affection for children appears, turn the light around and look: can this single recitation of the Buddha’s name really hold its own against this love? Can it really cut off this love? If it cannot cut off this love, how after all can birth and death be ended? Because the conditions of love have been familiar through many lives, while Buddha-recitation has only just been aspired to and is very unfamiliar, and is not earnest and solid besides, therefore it has no power.
[The conditions of love] The
conditions of affection. The Ratnakūṭa Sutra says: “Among all afflictions, that which is joined by the conditions of love is the heaviest.”

[If one cannot take charge of the objects of love before one now, then at the moment of death one certainly will not be able to take charge. Therefore I urge those who recite the Buddha’s name: first, one must know that the mind seeking to end birth and death must be urgent, and the resolve to cut off birth and death must be urgent; one must cut off thought after thought at the root-stock of birth and death, and then every thought is the time for ending birth and death. Why must one wait until the thirtieth day of the twelfth month to end it? That would be late indeed! As it is said: “Before your eyes all is the business of birth and death; if you can settle it before your eyes, birth and death are empty.” If one’s mindfulness is this earnest and every stroke draws blood, and one applies the mind in this way, then if one does not escape birth and death, all the Buddhas would have uttered false speech. Therefore, whether householder or monastic, one need only know the mind that seeks to end birth and death — that is the season for escaping birth and death. How could there be any other wondrous method!]

If one cannot take charge even of the objects of love before one now, then at the moment of death one certainly will not be able to take charge. Therefore I urge those who recite the Buddha’s name: first, one must understand that the resolve to cut off birth and death must be urgent. Understanding this, one must cut off thought after thought at the root of birth and death (the root of love); then every thought is the time for ending birth and death. Why must one wait until the thirtieth day of the twelfth month (the moment of death) to end birth and death? If only then does one think of ending birth and death, it is late indeed! As it is said: “Before your eyes all is the business of birth and death; if you can settle it before your eyes, birth and death are empty.” If one’s mindfulness is this earnest and every stroke draws blood, and one applies the mind in this way, then if one does not escape birth and death, all the Buddhas would have uttered false speech. Therefore, whether householder or monastic, one need only truly have the mind that seeks to end birth and death — that is the season for escaping birth and death. How could there be any other wondrous method!

[Before your eyes all is the business of birth and death; if you can settle it before your eyes, birth and death are empty] Before your eyes all is the business of birth and death; when you can settle these businesses of birth and death before your eyes, you settle birth and death (birth and death are empty).

[Severing love and focusing the thought] To cut off love and make one’s thought single. [To cut off love and make one’s thought single] To cut off the root of love and focus single-mindedly the thought of Buddha-recitation.
Master Youxi says in his Dharma Words on the Pure Land:

[Yet to speak of it is not hard; to practice it is hard. To practice it is not hard; to grasp the essential point of mind is hard. This is what the ancients warned of, and what we should observe. If one seeks the most earnest and true teaching for oneself, nothing is more essential than the two sayings of Yang Cigong: ‘If love is not heavy, one is not born in the Saha world; if thought is not single, one is not born in the Pure Land.’]

Yet as for this matter of seeking rebirth in the Pure Land, to speak of it is not hard; to practice it in fact is hard. To practice it in fact is not hard; to awaken to the essential point of practice is hard. This is what the ancients warned of, and we should reverently observe it. If one wishes to obtain the most earnest and true teaching for oneself on how to practice, nothing surpasses the two sayings of Yang Cigong: ‘If love is not heavy, one is not born in the Saha world; if thought is not single, one is not born in the Pure Land.’

[Yang Cigong] Yang Jie, courtesy name Cigong, style name Wuweizi. A man of the Song dynasty. He first delighted in the Chan school and awakened greatly through studying under Chan Master Tianyi Huai. At the end of the Xining reign he returned home on account of his mother’s mourning (his mother’s death), and in leisure read the Buddhist canon; thereupon he turned his heart to the Pure Land and advocated it vigorously, and he painted a sixteen-foot Amitābha Buddha to carry with him for contemplation. At the time of his death he saw a golden terrace come down from the sky, and he spoke a verse and passed away. [If love is not heavy, one is not born in the Saha world] To end birth and death and escape the round of rebirth, one must cut off love. The Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment says: “All sentient beings, from beginningless time, because of all kinds of affection, love, and desire, have the round of rebirth.” [If thought is not single, one is not born in the Pure Land] To attain rebirth in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss, one must focus single-mindedly the thought of Buddha-recitation. To focus single-mindedly the thought of Buddha-recitation is what the Chapter on the Perfect Penetration of Buddha-Recitation by Bodhisattva Mahāsthāmaprāpta calls “pure thoughts in succession,” and what Master Shandao calls “thought after thought without interruption.”

[Now, to recite the Buddha’s name in order to make one’s mind single, earnestly holding the name with undivided and undistracted purpose: this is what we should exert our hearts upon. Yet sometimes one forgets and cannot recite, or recites but cannot make it single — there is no other reason: one is pulled away by affection and love. To make light of love in order to block delusion, to cut off the root of affection, to escape the net of love: this is what we should exert our hearts upon. Yet sometimes one recites but cannot forget love, or forgets but cannot forget utterly — there is no other reason: the mind of recitation cannot be made single. Therefore, for one who recites the Buddha’s name and seeks rebirth in the Pure Land, if in ordinary times there is a single love of the Saha world that is not made light of, then at the moment of death one will be pulled away by that love and will not attain rebirth — how much more with many loves? And if in the Pure Land there is a single thought that is not single, then at the moment of death one will be turned about by that thought and will not attain rebirth — how much more with many thoughts?]

Reciting the Buddha’s name is for the sake of making the mind single. Therefore to hold the name earnestly, with single-minded devotion and no distraction, is what one ought to exert one’s heart upon. Yet sometimes one forgets and does not recite, or recites but cannot make it single; there is no other reason — one’s mind of Buddha-recitation has been pulled away by affection and love (and deluded thoughts arise). To make light of love in order to block deluded thought, to cut off the root of affection, to escape the net of love: this is what one ought to exert one’s heart upon. Yet sometimes one recites but cannot forget love, or wishes to forget love but cannot forget it utterly; there is no other reason — it is that the mind of Buddha-recitation cannot be made single. Therefore, for one who recites the Buddha’s name and seeks rebirth in the Pure Land, if in ordinary times there is a single love of the Saha world that is not let go, then at the moment of death one will be pulled away by that love and will not attain rebirth — how much more with many loves? If in seeking rebirth in the Pure Land there is a single thought that is not single, then at the moment of death one will be turned about by that thought which is not single and will not attain rebirth — how much more with many thoughts that are not single?
[Shen (shěn)] How much more.

[Now, as to what love is: it may be light or heavy, thick or thin; it may be direct retribution or circumstantial retribution. Enumerating its items: parents, wife and children, elder and younger brothers, friends, rank and wealth, essays and poems, arts and skills, clothing and food, houses and fields, springs and flowers, treasures and playthings — all kinds of wondrous and lovely things, too many to count. Some are great and heavy as Mount Tai, some small and light as a goose feather. To be unable to forget a single thing is love; to be unable to let go of a single thought is love. If a single love remains in the heart, the thought is not single; if a single thought does not return to oneness, one will not attain rebirth.]

And as to what love is: it may be light or heavy, thick or thin; it may be direct retribution or circumstantial retribution. Enumerating its kinds, there are parents, wife and children, brothers and friends, rank and wealth, essays and poems, arts and skills, clothing and food, houses and fields, springs and flowers, treasures and playthings, and all kinds of wondrous and lovely things — too many to list one by one. Among them, some are great and heavy as Mount Tai, some small and light as a goose feather. To be unable to forget a single thing is love; to be unable to let go of a single thought is love. If a single love remains in the heart, the thought of Buddha-recitation is not single; if a single thought does not return to oneness, one will not attain rebirth in the Pure Land.
[Elder and younger brothers] Brothers.

[Alas! ‘If love is not heavy, one is not born in the Saha world; if thought is not single, one is not born in the Pure Land’ — these two sayings may be called the golden lancet that scrapes the film from a clouded eye, the sacred medicine that cures a disease beyond cure. All who have the aspiration to seek rebirth in the Pure Land should write these words on their walls, engrave them on their flesh, solemnly recite them at all times, and keep them before the mind in every thought. With regard to the loves of the Saha world, seek daily to make them lighter; with regard to the thought of the Pure Land, seek daily to make it single. Lighter and still lighter, until one gradually reaches nothing; single and still more single, until one gradually draws near the utmost. If one can truly do this, then though this person has not yet escaped the Saha world, he is no longer a long-staying guest of the Saha world; though he is not yet born in the Pure Land, he is already an honored guest of the Pure Land. At the moment of death right mindfulness will appear before him, and rebirth in the Pure Land is certain.]

Alas! ‘If love is not heavy, one is not born in the Saha world; if thought is not single, one is not born in the Pure Land’ — these two sayings may be called the golden lancet that scrapes the film from a clouded eye, the sacred medicine that cures a disease beyond cure. All who have the aspiration to seek rebirth in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss should write these two sayings on their walls, engrave them on their flesh, solemnly recite them at all times, and keep them before the mind in every thought. With regard to the loves of the Saha world, seek daily to make them lighter; with regard to the thought of the Pure Land, seek daily to make it single. Love: lighter and still lighter, until one gradually reaches having none; thought: single and still more single, until one gradually reaches the utmost. If one can truly do this, then though this person has not yet escaped the Saha world, he is no longer a long-staying guest of the Saha world; though he is not yet born in the Pure Land, he is already an honored guest of the Pure Land. At the moment of death right mindfulness will appear before him, and rebirth in the Pure Land is certain.

[The golden lancet that scrapes the film from a clouded eye] Jin bi (pī), that is, jin bi (bī). This was a medical implement of ancient times, used to scrape away the film that covers the surface of the eyeball, thereby restoring sight. [Beyond cure] Refers to a terminal illness.

[Someone asked: Is there a way to make love light? The answer: For making love light, nothing is more essential than single thought. He asked again: Is there a way to make the thought single? The answer: For making the thought single, nothing is more essential than making love light. The man smiled and said: The Master’s words are like a rat peeping from its hole, first one end then the other; they seem to have no settled principle — how is the student to follow them? The answer: It is not two ends; I wish to make clear the reason why the thought is made single. For the thought cannot be made single because the scattered mind runs after alien conditions. The scattered mind and alien conditions in turn come about because one chases objects and races about in confusion. Therefore, where the Saha world has one object, sentient beings have one mind; where sentient beings have one mind, the Saha world has one object. Hence it is said: ‘Because mind arises, all kinds of dharmas arise; because dharmas arise, all kinds of mind arise.’ Gathering conditions and stirring within, racing outward in pursuit, mind and objects galloping together — dust-mote kalpas could not exhaust it. If love is not forgotten, can the thought be single?]

Someone asked: Is there a method for making love light? The answer: The most essential thing for making love light is to make one’s thought single. He asked again: Is there a method for making the thought single? The answer: The most essential thing for making the thought single is to make love light. The man laughed and said: Master, your words waver this way and that, with no settled view; how is the student to know which to follow? The answer: It is not wavering; I wish to make clear the reason why the thought is made single. For the thought (the thought of Buddha-recitation) cannot be made single because the mind is scattered and clings elsewhere. The mind is scattered and clings elsewhere in turn because one chases objects and races about in confusion. Therefore, where the Saha world has one object, sentient beings have one mind; where sentient beings have one mind, the Saha world has one object. Hence it is said: ‘Because mind arises, all kinds of dharmas arise; because dharmas arise, all kinds of mind arise.’ Conditions gather and the mind arises, chasing objects in flight; the mind clings to objects and objects pull the mind; mind and objects gallop together, and dust-mote kalpas cannot exhaust it. If love is not cut off, can the thought be single?
[If love is not forgotten] If love is not extinguished. In classical Chinese, “forget” is interchangeable with “perish,” meaning “to be extinguished.”

[Smiled] The appearance of smiling. [A rat peeping from its hole, first one end then the other] To waver between two sides. “A rat peeping”: the rat is by nature suspicious, and when coming out of its hole it pokes its head out and then draws it back; “two ends” means that whether to advance or retreat, no decision can be made.

Therefore, one who wishes to make his thought single had best make light of his love; one who wishes to make love light had best make his mind single. To make the mind single, one had best block out objects; when all objects are empty, the ten thousand conditions are all stilled; when the ten thousand conditions are all stilled, the single thought is accomplished of itself. If the single thought is accomplished, the conditions of love are all exhausted. Hence it is said: ‘To make the thought single, nothing surpasses making love light; to make love light, nothing surpasses the single thought.’ For love and thought cannot stand together, like day and night following one another, like light and dark turned away from each other.]

Therefore, one who wishes to make his thought single had best make light of his love; one who wishes to make love light had best make his mind single. To make the mind single, one had best block out objects (so that the mind does not cling to objects); when all objects are empty, the ten thousand conditions are all stilled; when the ten thousand conditions are all stilled, the single thought is accomplished of itself (the single, pure thought of the Buddha is naturally accomplished). If the single thought is accomplished, the conditions of love are all exhausted. Hence it is said: ‘To make the thought single, nothing surpasses making love light; to make love light, nothing surpasses the single thought.’ For love and singleness of thought cannot stand together, like night and day alternating with one another, or like darkness and light utterly opposed. (Therefore, cutting off love and singleness of thought support each other.)
Question: In letting go of the ten thousand conditions and single-mindedly reciting the Buddha’s name to seek rebirth in the Pure Land, is one concerned only with benefiting oneself?
Answer: Master Yinguang says:

“To wish to save others while unable to save oneself — how is that different from ferrying people while drowning in the sea? I urge you all: do not be puffed up with lofty self-conceit; better to have true faith and earnest vows, and relying on compassionate power, recite the Buddha’s name and seek rebirth in the West.”
